course.title: Mechanics of Materials
course.instructor_note: The instructor is identifiable from the FEA report template, and is the same instructor as ENGR 322. Rules the two packs share (hand-versus-FEA agreement, test corrections) therefore come from one source, not two. No name is recorded.

coverage.notes: Absence claims in this pack describe one search, not the world: a listing of this course's folders in the student's iCloud term archive and his university OneDrive, in September 2026. The FEA report is well covered. The instructor wrote a model report with placeholder values that sets its sections, its agreement target and its length. The lab-exercise prompts survive, and one completed report with its paired workbook survives. Everything else is thin. The test-correction memo has two instances and no prompt; one of the two is readable. The cantilever beam lab survives as a workbook plus a report that is almost all images. All 13 chapter problem sets are scanned handwriting with no text layer, so the homework format is not covered at all. There is no syllabus. Methods rest on the instructor's typed study guide, the FEA prompts and the student's test corrections. A second pass through the OneDrive copies found no new instructor-written material, so no level is raised. Those copies include five SolidWorks study folders (the plate, the axial and torsional wedding cake, and a class copy), which are native results files: they show what the student ran (mesh, displacement, strain and stress exports, solver output), not what a deliverable must show. The submitted report carries one result plot per exercise and no mesh or boundary-condition plots. The report and its workbook, not the study folders, are the source of the pressure-vessel pitfall (a sharper way the hand and FEA numbers can disagree without either being wrong), and the cantilever workbook and report are the source of the additions to the cantilever lab. All of it is observed once in one student's work.

course_policy.summary: No syllabus or generative-AI policy for this course was found in the student's iCloud term folders or his university OneDrive, searched September 2026.

format.deliverable: An FEA report comparing hand calculations with FEA, supported by a spreadsheet; a cantilever beam lab; test-correction memos; chapter problem sets.
precedence: the specific lab exercise or assignment prompt

artifacts.extension: SolidWorks part and simulation study (Inventor also accepted by one prompt)

pipeline_support.note: The report (docx/pdf) and a workbook (xlsx) are formats this repo renders, This pack states three format.rendering fields (no abstract, table captions above, figure captions below) and leaves the rest to renderer defaults; see rendering_basis. It sets no page budget or required figure roles. A placeholder test render confirmed the stated fields reach the renderer, but no render has been compared against the instructor's model report, so treat rendered output as unverified until inspected. The FEA results cannot be produced here: every FEA value and screenshot must come from the student's own study, and the report must not state agreement that was never measured.

rendering_basis.abstract: spec: the instructor's model FEA report opens with an Introduction and carries no abstract, and neither test-correction memo has one
rendering_basis.table_captions_above: spec: the instructor's model FEA report puts its table caption above the table's header row; every table in the student's FEA report does the same
rendering_basis.figure_captions_below: default, observed not stated: every figure in the student's FEA report has its caption below the image. The instructor's model only leaves blank space around a figure caption that follows the sentence introducing the plot, which fits but does not show it
rendering_basis.one_block_two_families: This pack holds one rendering block, but two families here render as documents: the FEA report and the test-correction memo. Only fields the two agree on are stated. Fields where they disagree are omitted and fall to the renderer's defaults, listed below with what each family shows.

omitted.title_page: They disagree. The instructor's model FEA report has a cover page (title, subtitle and byline on page 1, alone), and the student's report does too. Both test-correction memos start their text on page 1 under a one-line title.
omitted.number_body_pages: They disagree. The instructor's model FEA report numbers its body pages at the bottom right, starting at 1 on the first page after the cover. The test-correction memos carry no page numbers.
omitted.body_font_size: They disagree, and there is no written rule. The instructor's model FEA report is set in 11 pt Arial (measured); the student's memos use a 12 pt default.
omitted.margin_inches: They disagree, and there is no written rule. The instructor's model FEA report has 1.25 in side margins (measured); the student's memos and report use 1 in.
omitted.line_spacing: Not stated. The instructor's model report sets about 1.25 times the font size baseline to baseline (measured), but this renderer reads line_spacing as a leading ratio in PDF and as a Word multiple in docx, so no one value reproduces it in both.

fea_report: Each sheet holds an inputs table (Variable / Value / Units), with derived values computed by formula from the inputs.
Each sheet holds a comparison table (quantity / hand value / FEA value / percent difference) as an Excel table. FEA values are typed in from the simulation, and the percent difference is a formula.
FEA screenshots are pasted into the sheet beside the numbers.

The report transcribes both tables for each exercise as captioned Word tables, and the screenshots as captioned figures. The workbook is where the numbers come from; the report is where they are explained.
cantilever_lab: The pairing is reversed. The single worksheet holds the trials, their average, the FEA value, the percent error and a chart, and the typed answers to the handout's six guiding questions.
The report is almost entirely images: photos, ink and pasted content, around two question headings.
report_workbook_pairing.rule: The pairing is not uniform across assignments. Ask which file carries the answers before drafting either one.
report_workbook_pairing.source: two report-plus-workbook pairs in the OneDrive archive

title_block.placement: Alone on a cover page, centred. The body starts on the next page, which is numbered 1 in the instructor's model.
title_block.correction: An earlier version of this pack said the title block sat at the top of page 1 with no separate title page. That was wrong: the instructor's model report and the student's report both put it alone on a cover page.

sections: Procedure: how each model was built to match the hand-calculation assumptions (geometry, material, supports, loads)
one section per loading case: axial, torsional, pressure vessel, stress concentration, plus optional extra cases for bonus credit
Discussion: the lessons of the loading cases drawn into one theme. The instructor's model marks this as the most important section, and says criticism of the software or the process is acceptable.
Conclusion: a short restatement of the introduction and discussion, with a hint of how well the data agreed
loading_case_section: the governing hand equation, stated where first used
the FEA result and the hand result, in the text
a figure of the FEA result
a summary table: FEA value / hand value / percent difference
the cause of the difference, and which direction each method's approximation pushes the result
fea_report.agreement_target: about 5 percent or less; a larger difference is acceptable only if it is explained
fea_report.length: The instructor's model estimates roughly 3-15 pages of text and tables, and possibly double that with images.
fea_report.figures: Keep a figure only if the text relies on it, and give each one a single narrow job. Screenshots offered as proof of effort are cut. Describe simple setups in words, and picture only the loads or supports that words handle badly. Observed once, not stated by the instructor: the student's plate figure marks, with a probe callout (node, position, value), the points its tabulated FEA values were read from, and every result plot carries a legend with units. A figure that backs a tabulated number is easier to trust when the reader can see where the number was read. The same student's study exported mesh, strain and displacement plots that the report leaves out, which fits the model's rule to cut images that only show effort.
fea_report.captions: Figure N - description, below the figure; Table N - description, above the table.
fea_report.source: instructor model report + lab exercise prompts + student report

structure: a paragraph naming the specific error and why it happened
a paragraph on the concrete change of practice

methods.title: Validate a hand calculation with FEA
methods.when: Every FEA lab exercise and the FEA report.
methods.shared_with: engr322 (same instructor: one source, not independent agreement)
steps: Solve by hand with the course equation for the loading case, and list the assumptions it makes.
Build the FEA model to match those assumptions: the same geometry, material properties (E, G, Poisson's ratio), supports and load.

Compare the same quantity in the same units at the same location. Name the FEA result you read (a stress component, von Mises, or a resultant displacement) and pair it with the hand quantity of the same kind. For stepped shafts and 'wedding cake' bars, compare the total first, then each section if the totals disagree.
Tabulate hand value, FEA value and percent difference, and define the sign of the difference once.
Explain every difference over about 5 percent: coordinate system, a load or support that the model could not reproduce, mesh quality at a stress riser, or local effects near the load.
pitfalls: Comparing different quantities (an angle of twist against a linear displacement) and then trying to explain the resulting large 'error'.

Pressure vessels: the hand equations are in cylindrical coordinates and the FEA reports Cartesian components. Transform before comparing, and compare a hoop stress with the FEA hoop component, not with a von Mises plot. In a plate in tension the two coincide, but in a pressure vessel they do not: at the bore of a thick tube loaded only by internal pressure, von Mises differs from the hoop stress even in a perfect model (roughly 7 percent for a wall as thick as a scuba tank's, less for a thinner wall), and the sign of the gap depends on the axial stress the model carries (the axial stress is about zero with no end load, and von Mises then runs above the hoop stress). A von Mises value read against a hand hoop stress can therefore look like a small, reassuring agreement that is two different quantities. Read the hoop component, or compute the hand von Mises from the principal stresses, and say which. Observed once, in one student's tube comparison, whose figure was a von Mises plot; the reported agreement is consistent with that mismatch.
Trusting stresses right at the load application point or a sharp corner.

methods.title: Stress and strain transformation, principal values, Mohr's circle
methods.when: Rotating a 2-D state of stress or strain, and finding principal and maximum shear values.
steps: Draw the element and mark the given stresses with their signs.
Measure the angle from the x axis to the n axis, counter-clockwise positive (the course study guide's convention).
Apply the transformation equations, or construct Mohr's circle, to get the stresses on the rotated plane.
Find the principal stresses and their angle, and the maximum in-plane shear.
For strains, use the strain transformation equations, then convert to stress with the isotropic plane-stress relations.
pitfalls: Measuring the angle from n to x, or clockwise, which flips the sign of the shear term.
Mixing the plane-stress and plane-strain relations.

methods.title: Axial deflection, thermal strain and statically indeterminate bars
methods.when: Stepped bars, composite bars, bars between walls, and temperature change.
steps: Split the bar into sections of constant load, area and material.
Sum PL/(AE) over the sections for the total deflection.
For an indeterminate bar, write equilibrium plus a compatibility condition (equal strain, or deflections that sum to a known gap).
Add thermal strain alpha times delta T, positive for heating, by superposition.
pitfalls: A load that changes along the bar but is treated as constant.
A modulus entered with the wrong exponent sign in a table. It is harmless only while nothing uses the cell, so check every input's order of magnitude.

methods.title: Carry units through every line
methods.when: Always, especially with moments in foot-pounds and stresses in psi.
steps: Write units on every quantity in every line of the working.
Convert moments to inch-pounds before computing a stress in psi.
Sanity-check the magnitude of each answer before moving on.
pitfalls: Leaving a moment in foot-pounds inside a psi calculation, which is off by a factor of 12. Both of the student's test-correction memos trace lost points to exactly this.
Carrying one wrong unit from an early part into every later part that reuses it.

methods.title: Stress concentration at holes and fillets
methods.when: Plates with holes, stepped shafts, notches.
steps: Compute the nominal stress on the net section.
Read the concentration factor from the chart at this geometry's own ratio (hole diameter to width, fillet radius to diameter).
Multiply to get the peak stress, and compare it with the FEA maximum near the riser, after a mesh refinement there.
pitfalls: Reusing one concentration factor for two features with different ratios. The factors differ, and apparent FEA agreement does not make a shared factor right.
Hard-coding a rounded intermediate value into the comparison formula, which breaks the link to the inputs.

assignment_families.title: FEA experiments report (hand calculations versus FEA)
stages: weekly FEA lab exercises, each a short write-up with hand calculations and screenshots
a workbook of the inputs and comparison tables for each exercise
compilation into one report with a discussion and a conclusion
what_good_looks_like: Every loading case has its equation, a figure, a hand/FEA/percent table and an explanation of the difference.
Differences are within about 5 percent or explained with a specific cause.
The discussion draws the cases into one lesson about using FEA.
Every figure makes a point the text uses.
The numbers in the report match the workbook.
assignment_families.basis: instructor-written model report with placeholder values (strongest evidence), the lab-exercise prompts, one completed student report with its paired workbook. The same instructor sets the hand-versus-FEA rule in ENGR 322, so the two courses are one source.

assignment_families.title: Cantilever beam lab
stages: compare the measurements with hand calculation and FEA
answer the handout's six guiding questions
deliverables: workbook with trials, averages, FEA comparison, chart and answers
what_good_looks_like: Every one of the handout's six questions is answered: which material properties and beam dimensions to use, how to measure, how to build the setup, how to make it repeatable across beams, how well the hand calculation matches the FEA, and how well it matches the measurements.

The two 'how well' questions are answered with a percent difference and its likely cause. The one surviving answer to both says only that the match is 'pretty good', which is too thin to copy. The FEA report's habit (a number, then the cause of any gap) is the safer model, though the cantilever handout's own expectation is not known.

The hand model is tip deflection PL^3/(3EI) with I = bh^3/12. The surviving workbook backs the modulus out of each trial's measured deflection and averages the trials, then compares the FEA deflection with the measured average.
Beam thickness is measured for every trial. It enters I cubed, so a 3 percent thickness error becomes roughly a 9 percent error in the modulus backed out of the data.

The trials are screened before they are averaged. In the surviving workbook one of five deflection trials sits well above the other four and is averaged in without comment, which can change the reported agreement with the FEA severalfold. If a trial is dropped, say which and why.
assignment_families.basis: one completed group workbook (trials, average, FEA deflection, percent error, chart, typed answers) and an image-only report made of screenshots of that workbook and of the FEA displacement plot. No handout text survives beyond the six question headings. Everything in the list above is observed once, in work that may be a draft, except the questions themselves, which appear to be copied from the handout. The report's format is not covered.

assignment_families.title: Test-correction memo

what_good_looks_like: Each missed problem names the specific error (the step, the unit, the misread given), not a general cause.
Each has a concrete change of practice for the next test.

assignment_families.title: Chapter problem sets
assignment_families.basis: 13 sets, all scanned handwriting with no text layer. Nothing about their format is covered, and none is inferred.

magnitudes.quantity: percent difference between hand calculation and FEA for the same quantity at the same location
magnitudes.basis: Handout: the instructor's model FEA report says overall differences should be 5% or less, or be explained, and that pressure-vessel differences may run higher. The upper bound of 10 is a plausibility margin above that target, not a course rule.
magnitudes.note: Tens of percent or more usually means different quantities are being compared (angle of twist against a displacement), a different location, a coordinate mismatch (cylindrical vs Cartesian in a pressure vessel), or a stress read at a singular node. Exactly 12x or 1/12x: a moment left in ft-lb.

magnitudes.quantity: computed working stress divided by the material's yield strength
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: homework and lab parts are loaded to stay elastic, so working stress is a fraction of yield. Above 1 the part would yield and the linear equations no longer apply.
magnitudes.note: Well above 1: check the moment units first. A moment left in ft-lb inside a psi formula is 12x too small, and the reverse slip 12x too large. A ratio range cannot see every 12x slip, so check the moment units on every line anyway.

magnitudes.quantity: modulus of elasticity of a common structural metal (input)
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: about 10 x 10^6 psi for aluminum and 29-30 x 10^6 psi for steel. Handbook values.
magnitudes.note: Off by powers of ten: the exponent in a table cell has the wrong sign or size. It is harmless only while no formula reads the cell, so check the order of magnitude of every input. This range is for metals. The cantilever lab uses a thin wooden strip whose modulus is roughly a tenth of steel's, so a low value there is not a slip and this range does not apply to it.

magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: steels and aluminum alloys sit near 0.3, cast irons nearer 0.2-0.26, and any isotropic material lies between 0 and 0.5.
magnitudes.note: Outside 0-0.5: not a Poisson's ratio. The shear modulus G and E were probably swapped somewhere.

magnitudes.quantity: normal strain in an elastic member
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: metals yield at strains of roughly 0.001 to 0.005, so elastic working strains are below that.
magnitudes.note: Above about 0.005: the member would have yielded, or a length is in inches against a modulus in ksi. Hundreds or thousands: strain reported in microstrain without saying so.

magnitudes.quantity: stress concentration factor Kt read from a chart
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: Kt is peak over nominal stress, so it is at least 1, and holes and fillets within the chart ranges give roughly 1.2 to 3.
magnitudes.note: Below 1: impossible, so the chart was read at the wrong ratio or the wrong curve. The same Kt for two features with different ratios is suspect even when it lands in range.

magnitudes.quantity: coefficient of thermal expansion of a metal (input)
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: about 6.5 x 10^-6 /degF for steel and 13 x 10^-6 /degF for aluminum. Handbook values.
magnitudes.note: About 1.8x high: a per-degC value used with degF. Powers of ten off: the exponent.
